summary: Awbrey Butte was proposed for a fire lookout and observatory in 1919; a Deschutes County blog says no structure was built, and the summit is now fenced.

facts.status_note: No tower was built here, according to a Deschutes County lookouts blog; the site was used for fire detection.

access.note: The summit is fenced to protect communications towers. Hiking routes follow the fence and do not reach the top (Oregon Hikers guide).

visit.trail_note: No tower to climb. The hiking route runs along the summit fence and then down through neighborhoods, mostly on sidewalks.

events.note: Proposed as a combined observatory and fire lookout, with a 40-ft tower planned and a 50-ft tower later mentioned. The Deschutes County blog gives 1919 as the construction date but records no structures built.
Forest service men at headquarters saw a blaze in private timber from the top of Awbrey Heights (Bend Bulletin item dated July 31, 1919).

evidence.supports: 1919 proposal for a combined observatory and fire lookout, contingent on a donated lot
evidence.quote: If some property owner on Awbrey heights will donate the use of a lot to the forest service, Bend will have a combination observatory and fire lookout this summer.

evidence.supports: Judge J.A. Estes named as offering a lot (April 18, 1919 item)
evidence.quote: Judge J.A. Estes has offered to donate to the Deschutes National Forest

evidence.supports: Planned 40-ft tower and auto road to its base
evidence.quote: the forest service will build a 40-foot tower and will build and maintain a first class auto road to the base of the tower

evidence.supports: Site on property owned by Mrs. V.A. Forbes (July 15, 1919 item)
evidence.quote: on property owned by Mrs. V.A. Forbes

evidence.supports: Judge Estes negotiating for permission to install a 50-ft tower
evidence.quote: Judge Estes is now negotiating with the owner for permission to install a 50-foot tower.

evidence.supports: July 31 item: the 50-ft tower will be erected in the near future
evidence.quote: A 50-foot tower will be erected in the near future, it is expected.

evidence.supports: Blaze seen from the top of Awbrey Heights
evidence.quote: forest service men stationed at headquarters here were able to observe from the top of Awbrey Heights a blaze in the privately owned timber southwest of Lava Butte.

evidence.supports: Heavy smoke kept the other lookouts from locating fires
evidence.quote: were unable to locate fires Tuesday afternoon because of heavy smoke

evidence.supports: Blog gives 1919 as construction date but no structures built

evidence.quote: Was used for fire detection, at least one recorded report.

evidence.supports: Plans were for a fire tower and a visitors viewpoint
evidence.quote: Plans were for a fire tower and visitors view point.

evidence.supports: Awbrey Butte rises above Bend's north side
evidence.quote: Awbrey Butte dominates Bend’s northern skyline

evidence.supports: Summit fenced, protecting communications towers; no route to the top
evidence.quote: You can’t actually get to the top of Awbrey Butte: the summit is surrounded by a fence that protects an array of communications towers.

evidence.supports: Descent to the Deschutes mostly on sidewalks
evidence.quote: The descent to the Deschutes is mostly on sidewalks.

corrections.why: The blog says no structures were built and the site was used for fire detection. The 'point' kind is a bare lookout point with no structure.
12.2 m (40 ft) is the height of the 1919 proposed tower, not a built height. The blog says no structures were built.

resolved_conflicts.explanation: The 1919 newspaper items describe plans for a 40-ft and then a 50-ft tower. The blog gives 1919 as the construction date but pairs it with 'No structures built', so this research treats the tower as never built and 1919 as the planning date.

sources.title: Bend (Awbrey Butte), Forest Lookouts (1919 Bend Bulletin items)

notes_for_editor: The 'no structure built' finding rests on one blog entry. The 1919 Bend Bulletin items describe plans only, and no later item in the Oregon Lookouts file reports a tower going up. The record's status stays 'unknown' because no status value means 'never built'. The 'point' kind and the height correction are proposals for a human to review. The access note rests on one hiking guide. Fact-check 2026-10-21: the hiking guide is cited for the fence, the communications towers and the sidewalk descent. The guide's text does not mention a lookout; that is a reading of the whole page, not a quotable fact.
